newsitem.title: PERU: Fujimori returns to reality of Peru siege standoff.
newsitem.headline: Fujimori returns to reality of Peru siege standoff.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori returned to the grim reality of Peru's deadlocked hostage crisis on Wednesday after two days of distractions offered by the visit of Ecuador's energetic leader Abdala Bucaram.

While Fujimori raced around Lima and the provinces with Bucaram on Tuesday, earning support from cheering crowds and praise from the Ecuadoran president, the standoff with Marxist rebels at the besieged Japanese ambassador's home showed no sign of easing.

The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels holding 74 hostages have not replied to the government's proposal on Sunday that a "guarantors commission" oversee new face-to-face talks between the sides.

Negotiations scheduled for Sunday collapsed before starting because the rebels insisted the meeting be centred on their demand for the release of more than 400 jailed comrades -- which Fujimori has refused to consider.
Fujimori's tough line was praised by Bucaram.
"The world supports Peru and its president not backing down in its position, because it would set a very bad precedent to negotiate with people who employ chaos and violence," he said.
With the stalled talks pointing to a protracted standoff, police tried to tighten security around the besieged diplomatic mansion.

Police chief Col. Fernando Zapata warned members of the Japanese media on Tuesday not to attempt to enter the captured residence again. Zapata said two Asian-looking journalists were reported early on Tuesday to have been hanging around a nearby house from where two members of Japan's TV Asahi managed to sneak past police and into the residence on Jan. 7.
Suspected sniper fire from outside the residence whizzed above the heads of a group of journalists camped out on Tuesday on the roof of a neighbouring house overlooking the residence.
Fujimori left Lima on Tuesday for the first time since Dec. 17, when 15 heavily armed rebels stormed a lavish reception at the residence, taking more than 500 hostages.

He visited the site of one of his main victories against leftist rebels -- the village of Vilcashuaman in the mountain province of Ayacucho, a former centre of guerrilla activity that has been placed back under government control -- and proclaimed no one in the country supported the rebels.

"All Peruvians have clearly demonstrated that the people reject violence," Fujimori told a cheering crowd against the dramatic Andean backdrop. "All of Peru is against this hostage-taking and demands their freedom."

Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, a close friend of the president named by the Vatican to sit on the proposed guarantor commission, travelled with Fujimori and called on all sides to sit down for talks as soon as possible.

"My constant request is that God move everyone as soon as possible to start a dialogue which surely will bring peace," Cipriani said. "Please, trusting in God, trusting in truth and openness, sit down to talk. We wish for this, and I believe it will soon happen."

Red Cross spokeswoman Cecilia Baux told Reuters the organisation would join the commission if and when it is formally set up. "We can participate in the commission but only in matters of a humanitarian nature," she said.
The government and MRTA would fill the final two places on the commission proposed by the government.

The MRTA have released the majority of their hostages in what they called "goodwill gestures." They have kept dozens of top Peruvian government and security force officials, the younger brother of Fujimori, and Japanese diplomats and businessmen as bargaining chips to secure the release of their jailed comrades.
The rebels are armed with rifles and grenades and have booby-trapped and mined the compound against surprise attack.
